blocks.text: In this whole discussion I would think Bochart more successful in refuting the fancies of others than in establishing his own opinion. For at the beginning of this chapter he rightly objected to those who render it swallow, as if it were named from freedom, that this reason is not sufficient, since there are also other birds, some domestic, some wild; yet soon he himself uses the same reason to show that דרור is a species of wild dove. Indeed, our author's whole argument comes to this: the Hebrew דרור, like the Arabic حرّ [ḥurr], means free; but among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is an epithet of the wild dove; therefore the Hebrew דרור, carrying the same notion of freedom, denotes that same animal. How weak this is, anyone understands at once, since among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is not the name of the dove but an epithet of the wild dove, added to the noun ساق [sāq], which signifies the male dove. As for the two passages in which the word דרור occurs, we have seen (note 1 and 3) that the swallow fits the former (Proverb. XXVI, 2.) well enough, while for the other the swallow suits as well as the dove. — Forsskål, in Descript. Animalium in Itinere Orientali observatorum p. 10, mentions among the migratory birds of Alexandria one named Dururi, which comes when the dates have ripened, at the end of October, from Upper Egypt, and, when these have been consumed, leaves after three months. Since Alexandria is not much further south than Jerusalem, Michaelis (in Supplemm. vol. 2, p. 477) suspects that this bird may be the Hebrew דרור; yet he determines nothing certain, since it is doubtful in which letters the name is written in Arabic, دُرُوري [durūrī] or ضُرُوري [ḍurūrī]. Nevertheless, toward the end he adds: “Is it the species of sparrow, of the colour of a nightingale, with a very sweet song, which Shaw saw around Capsa in palm-bearing places, p. 185, Travels, German trans. 164? See also Buffons Naturgeschichte der Voegel vol. 10, p. 161, German trans. Thus I could have called it Dattelnsperling.” Although Michaelis proposed this with hesitation, Ziegler nevertheless took it as certain, in his translation of Proverbs. — Finally, Paulus, in Clavis Psalmorr. p. 209, flatly denies that any bird at all is denoted by the word דרור, because it is contrasted with τῷ [tō] צפור, that is, with the whole class of birds. Hence he himself renders the Hebrew word tiny ant, comparing the Arabic ذرّ [dharr]; see Castell [II, 596] Lexic. Hexapl. p. 77c. But צפור signifies both any birds whatever and specifically the sparrow. An ant, moreover, would hardly fit the passage Proverb. XXVI, 2. (דרור לעוף). Nor can a nest, קן, be attributed to an ant, as is done in Psal. LXXXIV, 4. — I would believe that דרור is an onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικον [onomatopoiētikon]) name of the turtledove, since all the ancient translators agree on this.
